ds: Specialists who launder criminal proceeds for others as a service, for a fee or commission, using networks of couriers, brokers, front companies, accounts and informal value transfer. They run structured, repeatable laundering infrastructure serving multiple criminal clients.

src.t: FATF, Professional Money Laundering (2018); FATF and Egmont, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)
Europol, European Union Serious and Organised Crime Threat Assessment (EU SOCTA) (specify 2021 or 2025)
FATF, Investigating Professional Money Laundering, Underground Banking, and the Use of Hawala and Other Similar Service Providers (2026-09-03)

cn.rt: Professional launderers recruit or run multiple personal accounts for third-party flows with fee retention; commercial and trade elements excluded.

rat: Specialist networks use front-company accounts, MSBs, couriers and informal value transfer with mirror transactions across jurisdictions.

ind.n: Accounts serving many unrelated clients with common controller
ind.cx: Multiple accounts or companies linked to the same controllers are used for flows of different, unrelated parties.
ind.fp: Payment agents and accountants hold client money legitimately.
ind.ds: Several apparently separate businesses or sub-accounts share owners, signatories, addresses, devices or bank accounts.

ind.n: Funds move in fixed commission-like deductions
ind.cx: Recurring small percentage retained from inbound flows consistent with fee-taking by an intermediary.
ind.fp: Brokers and payment agents charge fees.
ind.ds: Recurring small percentage retained from inbound flows consistent with fee-taking by an intermediary.

ind.n: Mirror or offsetting transactions between jurisdictions
ind.cx: Payments in one country are balanced by payments elsewhere without movement of funds between them.
ind.fp: Netting and bank-to-bank settlement may look similar.
ind.ds: Reciprocal or offsetting payments occur between counterparties or operators in different countries with no direct value transfer.

ind.n: Use of numerous shell companies with generic activity
ind.cx: Large number of newly formed companies cycle funds with vague trade descriptions.
ind.ds: Recently incorporated entity or group of entities with generic business descriptions shows significant turnover or purchases soon after formation.
ind.cn: Newly formed entity with vague purpose and large flows

ind.n: Third-party payments for unrelated debts or purchases
ind.cx: Payers settle obligations of others without clear relationship, often in trade or loan context.
ind.fp: Guarantors or group treasury pay for others.
ind.ds: Funds are paid or received, or instructions are given to pay, through parties with no evident link to the customer, contract, debt or insured interest. Includes third-party cheques, loan repayments, premiums, gaming funds and goods payments not matching the documentation.
ind.cn: Payments from or to unrelated third parties

ind.n: Links to known launderers or adverse media
ind.cx: Counterparties or controllers appear in law-enforcement notices, adverse media or intelligence.
ind.ds: Counterparties, suppliers, respondents or controllers appear in adverse media, law-enforcement notices or intelligence connected to financial crime, abuse, forced labour or organised crime.
ind.cn: Adverse media or intelligence linking counterparties to criminal activity

ind.n: Complex use of multiple services for single flow
ind.cx: One flow touches cash, remitters, trade invoices, crypto and corporate accounts in a short time.
ind.ds: One flow touches cash, remitters, trade invoices, crypto and corporate accounts in a short time.

ind.n: Customer lacks understanding of the transactions it executes
ind.cx: Controllers cannot explain commercial purpose or counterparties.
ind.ds: When asked about a transaction, the customer gives vague, rehearsed, inconsistent or shifting explanations of its purpose, source or counterparties.
ind.cn: Unable or unwilling to explain transaction purpose or origin

ind.n: Frequent use of cash couriers or exchange houses alongside bank flows
ind.cx: Cash movement is blended with bank transfers via associated money service businesses.
ind.fp: MSB use is common in some communities.
ind.ds: Account activity regularly blends MSB, exchange house or cash courier movements with bank transfers.
ind.cn: Frequent use of money service businesses, exchange houses or cash couriers alongside bank flows

ctl.n: Client money account verification and rules
ctl.ds: Confirms legitimate client-account status and licensing and applies professional client-money rules, alerting on flows lacking a matter reference. It prevents professional accounts being used to move funds without underlying services.
Links accounts, devices, addresses, directors and beneficiaries to surface rings, shared attributes and flow structures that single-account views miss. It supports detection of organised networks.
Alerts when inflows are quickly moved out with little retained balance, including cash-in fast-out and rapid conversion or cash-out. It reveals accounts used as conduits for layering.
Risk-based vetting of intermediaries, brokers, partners and suppliers covering ownership, experience, references, public-official links and selection rationale. It limits exposure through proxies.

Detects funds that return to their origin or loop between linked parties through reciprocal, matched, netted or round-trip flows using graph analysis and account comparison. It exposes artificial turnover and loan-back structures.

Translates published and sanitised typologies and red flags into targeted monitoring scenarios and context-aware rules that are reviewed periodically. It aligns monitoring with known criminal methods.

Requires a documented commercial or legal reason for each layer of a multi-tier or cross-border structure, with specialist review and sign-off before approval. Unexplained complexity is treated as a risk driver and can lead to decline.

Tests whether an entity has real operations such as premises, staff, stock and contracts through documents, site or virtual visits, open-source footprint and shell-risk indicators. It helps identify shell and front companies with no genuine activity.

Detects, restricts and challenges payments or deposits made by or to parties not named in the contract, account or invoice, and requires evidence of the relationship. It stops accounts and trades being funded by unexplained third parties.

Runs continuous screening of customers, owners, introducers, suppliers and counterparties against curated news, leaks, regulatory notices and enforcement releases, with reliability grading and identity disambiguation. It surfaces negative information that registers and lists do not carry.
Participates in sector, regulator and public-private forums and platform cooperation to receive and share typologies and indicators where lawful. It keeps scenarios current.

Aggregates cash and other activity by customer, related party, account, branch, channel and day so that splitting across touchpoints cannot evade review, supported by a single customer view. It gives analysts a holistic picture of exposure.

Investigates linked clusters and networks of accounts as one case, including broker networks and accounts connected to seizures or requests, rather than reviewing accounts individually. It disrupts organised activity that single-account review would miss.

Trains branch, contact-centre and relationship staff to ask open questions, recognise coaching, coercion, pressure and evasion and escalate with authority to pause. It strengthens the human control at the point of contact.

ctl.n: Purpose and intended nature of relationship
ctl.ds: Captures and challenges the stated purpose of the account, expected activity, volumes and geographies at onboarding, creating a baseline against which later behaviour is judged. Vague or implausible answers prompt further enquiry or decline.
Reconciles cash, stock purchases, sales and exports with declared business activity to test whether deposits are plausible. It is used to identify unrecorded or injected cash.

Applies targeted enhanced checks to customer types or sectors known to be vulnerable to misuse, such as cash-intensive trades, money service businesses, high-value dealers, professional services, charities or waste handlers. Questions and evidence are tailored to how the sector normally operates.
